title: How to reduce moiré in clothing photos
description: Identify false waves or colors in fabric, compare the source and export, and try a local correction without erasing the garment’s texture.
summary: A garment-first workflow for handling false repeating patterns while preserving real weave, seams and color.
quickAnswer: Check the garment in the original at 100% view and in the final-size export. If false waves or colors remain, try a local moiré adjustment where your editor provides one. Keep the correction confined to the affected fabric and compare seams and genuine colors before deciding it helped.
imageAlt: Woman in a pink shirt and red cap leaning through an open window
caption: Illustrative stock photograph; not a Meluvya result or a test of the technique.

sections.title: Recognize a false pattern in a real pattern
paragraphs: Nikon explains moiré as a new pattern formed when a subject’s fine repeating detail interacts with the camera’s sampling pattern. Woven fabric is a common example. It can create distracting shapes or false color even when the garment itself does not contain them.

Compare with what you know about the clothing. A rainbow-like patch on a plain fine weave deserves investigation; an actual printed stripe should not be removed just because it is repetitive. If you can check another frame or the garment itself, use that reference.
Keep this separate from random speckles in a dark photograph. A noise-cleanup approach may not address the repeating structure that is bothering you.

sections.title: Compare source, preview and delivery
paragraphs: Inspect the original at 100% magnification, as Nikon recommends for evaluating the artifact, and also look at the intended display size. Open the exported file separately. Do not decide solely from a small editing preview.

If the troubling pattern changes dramatically between viewing sizes or appears only in the resized delivery, make a second export from the same clean master and compare the actual results. That observation helps locate the problem; it does not prove that the original contains no artifact.
Keep the image content and edit consistent during this comparison. Changing the crop, detail settings and export dimensions together makes it difficult to know which decision helped.

sections.title: Try a local correction on the cloth
paragraphs: Adobe documents a Moiré control among Lightroom mobile’s local adjustment options. Availability and placement should be checked against the editor and version you use.

items.title: Select the affected area.
items.text: Use a mask limited to the problematic fabric. Include the visible problem without unnecessarily covering skin, jewelry or surrounding objects.

items.title: Make a restrained trial.
items.text: Increase the relevant correction gradually while watching the false pattern. Avoid treating the slider’s maximum as a target.

items.title: Inspect real garment detail.
items.text: Compare seams, buttons, folds and any genuine color variation. Check that the apparent improvement has not turned the material into an indistinct patch.

items.title: Reopen the final export.
items.text: Judge the delivered size as well as a close view. Save the editable version so a later delivery size can be assessed independently.

sections.title: Use another capture when it is the better option
paragraphs: For an important garment photograph, compare nearby frames before spending a long time repairing one. Nikon notes that changing the relationship between camera and subject, including angle or focal length, can alter the occurrence of moiré.

A practical retake exercise is to preserve the garment’s pose and lighting while making a small viewpoint change, then compare the fabric carefully. For a portrait, keep the face usefully focused; sacrificing the whole subject’s clarity is not an attractive default solution to a shirt problem.
For an online listing, the weave and color may be essential information. A cleaner alternate frame can be more honest and more useful than a heavily smoothed version of the troublesome one.

sections.title: Accept the limits of a correction
paragraphs: Look separately at the false color and the false pattern. A result can improve one while leaving the other noticeable. If acceptable correction requires removing the garment’s real character, choose another image or revise the capture.
Keep the original and label the finished version clearly. Do not describe a reconstructed or strongly altered fabric as an accurate record of its texture when you cannot verify that claim.

faq.question: Is moiré the same as digital noise?
faq.answer: No. This guide concerns a false repeating pattern or color associated with fine detail. Random speckles and blotches require a separate diagnosis.

faq.question: Will desaturating the shirt fix every case?
faq.answer: It may hide a colored symptom while leaving a false brightness pattern, and it can change the garment’s true color. Compare a dedicated local correction or another frame first.
